name: Lemon juice whitening
lead: Lemon juice whitening is a home practice of applying lemon juice, alone or mixed with baking soda, to the teeth to remove stains. It is shared as a natural bleaching method.

Lemon juice is about 5 to 6% citric acid, with more than lime and several times more than orange juice [1]. Dental sources associate acidic foods and drinks, including citrus, with dental erosion [2]. No clinical trials of lemon juice as a tooth whitener were found.

paras: Proponents say the acid and the fruit's reputation as a natural bleach lighten tooth colour. Lemon juice is described in general sources as being used to lighten hair in sunlight [1], and some extend the idea to teeth. The encyclopedic lemon article does not mention teeth [1].
No studies found. Whitening trials in humans have tested peroxide products [4].

Dental erosion is irreversible loss of tooth structure by non-bacterial acids. Citrus fruit and fruit juices are discussed among dietary causes, with frequency of exposure and swishing acidic liquids increasing risk [2]. When enamel is lost and dentin is exposed, dentin hypersensitivity can result, and dental guidance includes limiting acidic foods and waiting before brushing [3].
Lemon juice and baking soda is a recurring item in natural whitening roundups. No community-sourced material was available for citation here.

card.summary: Lemon juice on teeth is a popular natural whitening idea; no trials were found and citric acid is a known erosion factor.
card.note: Citric acid is associated with enamel erosion.

quick.overview:
Lemon juice whitening means putting lemon juice, sometimes with baking soda, on the teeth to remove stains.

No clinical trials were found. Lemon juice is highly acidic, and dental sources link acidic foods and juices to enamel erosion.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say citric acid bleaches or dissolves stains. No research tests this; acids are also the mechanism of dental erosion.
quick.risks: Erosion is irreversible and may expose dentin, causing sensitivity. Dental sources note exposure frequency matters.
